cycles are unique substructures present in diverse natural
and bioactive molecules.<sup>1</sup> Owing to the high ring strain and
two reactive C = C bonds, they also have broad applications in
organic synthesis.<sup>2</sup> The
cycloaddition of allenes<sup>3</sup> and
alkynes<sup>4</sup> represents arguably the most direct approach to
access 3-alkylidenecyclobutenes (Scheme 1a).<sup>5−9</sup> However,
both allenes and alkynes have reactive π-systems that can
undergo homo- and cross-
and
cycloadditions, with the latter leading to more stable 6-
membered (often aromatic) products.<sup>10,11</sup> Moreover, for
terminal alkynes, hydroalkynylation of allenes is another well-
known process, which may lead to multiple regio- and
stereoisomers.<sup>12,13</sup> Therefore, the chemoselective generation
of a highly strained cross-[2 + 2] cycloadduct among so many
thermodynamically favorable pathways represents a formidable
challenge. Consequently, although this process has been
known for over a half century, limited success has been
achieved regarding substrate generality, eficiency, regioselec-
tivity, and mild conditions. If fact, current success has been
largely limited to activated substrates (e.g., electron-rich allenes
and electron-poor alkynes)<sup>6</sup> and/or intramolecular processes,
where the electronic bias or geometric constraints help simplify
the complications.
Indeed, there has been almost no progress in developing
eficient intermolecular
cycloadditions between
unactivated allenes and alkynes.<sup>8,9</sup>

allenes and alkynes are unsymmetrical but lack electronic
bias, controls over regioselectivity are required, which
constitutes another substantial challenge (Scheme 1b).

Next, we examined the alkyne scope (Scheme 2). Various
terminal alkynes substituted with alkyl-, alkenyl-, and aryl-
groups all eficiently reacted smoothly to furnish the
corresponding cyclobutenes, favoring the hindered isomer
with exceptional regioselectivity (3a−3w). The mild con-
ditions tolerated diverse functional groups, including silyl,
germanyl, halide, nitrile, (thio)ether, mesyl, acetal, ketone,
ester and even free alcohol. Electron-rich aryl acetylenes also
showed good reactivity, although they are known to deactivate
the catalyst by π-coordination. 1,4-Diethynylbenzene under-
went double cycloaddition successfully (3x). This protocol was
also applicable to internal alkynes, maintaining the unusual
excellent regioselectivity (3y−3ag). Complex alkynes derived
from active pharmaceutical molecules also reacted with equally
high eficiency. Of note, some products were generated in low
yield (e.g., 3l, 3m, 3ac) due to oligomerization of the alkyne
partne

these reactions. The low yield of 3t might be related to the

of 3ag was unambiguously confirmed by X-ray crystallography.
2D NMR and NOE studies were also performed on other
representative products.

and 1,1-disubstituted allenes with aryl and alkyl groups all led
to the desired products (4a−4m) with moderate to good
eficiency and excellent regioselectivity (Scheme 3). Increasing
the size of the substituents (4k−4m) had no detrimental efect.

details).

Control experiments and kinetic studies were performed to
help understand the mechanism (Figure 1). The reaction of 1e
with deuterated phenylacetylene aforded 4d-d with complete
D-incorporation at the same carbon without scrambling
(Figure 1a). Moreover, a mixture of two diferent aryl alkynes,
one of which was deuterated, resulted in a mixture without
intermolecular deuterium crossover. These observations
suggested that the cleavage of C(sp)−H bond may not be
involved, thus distinct from allene hydroalkynylation.<sup>12,13</sup> To
know more about the relationship between regioselectivity and
the alkyne size, we made a plot between the observed
regioisomeric ratio (rr) and the A-value of the alkyne
substituent. In fact, a reverse linear relationship was observed
(Figure 1b), suggesting that the bulkier alkyne tends to give a
lower regioisomeric ratio (e.g., rr = 2 for <sup>t</sup>Bu group, more
details in the SI).

catalyst (Figure 1c), implying that the catalyst might be
saturated by the two substrates by forming a stable complex,
serving as the catalyst resting state before the rate-determining
step.
